name: Clavicular's looksmaxxing philosophy

chain: Pursuit of a sharper face and physique
angle.text: Followers of streamer Clavicular treat his approach as a template for maximal 'ascension', combining drug protocols, bonesmashing talk and extreme self-improvement in pursuit of a more striking face and physique. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources have criticised the approach.

summary: The aggressive 'ascension' approach promoted by streamer Clavicular, spanning steroids, peptides and bonesmashing talk, with heavy criticism from medical sources.
note: Medical sources describe bonesmashing as pseudoscientific; legal allegations against the streamer are unproven and denied.
currentQuick:
Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Peters, an American streamer who became prominent in 2025 and 2026 on Kick and TikTok promoting extreme looksmaxxing. Wikipedia lists the practices he promotes as bonesmashing, anabolic steroids, methamphetamine for appetite suppression, and a paid course including guides on injectable peptides.
He is linked in media coverage to more extreme looksmaxxing and blackpill ideas. He denies that looksmaxxing is tied to incel culture.
How it works: His approach is described as 'hardmaxxing': drug and injectable use, extreme dieting and physical modification, packaged as a paid course. Bonesmashing involves hitting facial bones to reshape the jaw and is described by medical sources as pseudoscientific.
Risks and caveats: Critics argue his content harms young men, and Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says he overdosed on a livestream in 2026 after a five-drug 'pentastack'. Legal matters reported include arrests and charges, some dropped; a September 2026 Massachusetts charge is an allegation he denies.
deepLead:
Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Eric Peters, an American influencer born in December 2005 and raised in Hoboken, New Jersey, who gained prominence through livestreams and clips on Kick and TikTok in 2025 and 2026 . He promotes looksmaxxing, a trend of methods for improving appearance, and is associated with more extreme 'ascension' practices .
Practices Wikipedia attributes to his content include bonesmashing, anabolic steroids, methamphetamine used to suppress appetite, and a paid course originally called the Clavicular System, which includes guides on injectable peptides . name: Looksmax.org / forum participation

chain: Post photos and get PSL ratings
Apply tips to face and body
angle.text: Members use the forum to post progress photos, request ratings and swap guides, treating the feedback and shared methods as a map for improving their looks. The feedback comes from peers on a self-devised rating scale, and the guides' methods vary from studied to anecdotal.

summary: The main forum hub of looksmaxxing culture, where members post progress photos, seek PSL ratings and swap guides.
note: Community norms include PSL ratings and unverified methods; researchers and media have raised mental health and radicalisation concerns.
currentQuick:
Looksmax.org is described as one of the main later hubs of looksmaxxing, alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com. Members post guides, request ratings and share progress photos, often giving a current and 'potential' PSL score.
The forum scene traces back to mid-2010s boards such as Lookism.net and Sluthate, and moved to independent forums after platform bans, before spreading to TikTok around 2020.
How it works: Participation typically means posting photos for rating, discussing softmaxxing (non-invasive changes) and hardmaxxing (surgery, steroids), and using shared vocabulary such as canthal tilt and hunter eyes. Anonymity is common and members gatekeep against casual 'normies'.
Risks and caveats: Commentators and researchers link the subculture to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety, promotion of unproven or dangerous methods, blackpill determinism, and radicalisation. Critics also call the PSL scale unscientific and biased against non-white men.
deepLead:
Looksmax.org is an online forum that Grokipedia describes as one of the main later hubs of looksmaxxing, together with forum.looksmaxxing.com, hosting guides, PSL rating threads and rate-me requests . Looksmaxxing, a practice focused on maximising male attractiveness, formed on incel-linked message boards in the 2010s, and Wikipedia names PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net as the 'PSL forums' that created the PSL rating scale .
Wikipedia's article does not mention looksmax.org specifically, so the details below about it rest mostly on Grokipedia, an AI-generated source. Female-oriented guides reportedly appeared on the site in 2024 and 2025 .

name: Dopamine / porn avoidance

angle.text: Followers of NoFap and dopamine fasting abstain in the belief that it raises testosterone, focus and confidence, which they say make a person come across as more attractive. Researchers describe these specific appearance and hormone claims as unsupported, though dopamine fasting was developed as a behavioural tool.

summary: Abstaining from porn, masturbation or other stimulation to 'reset' dopamine, popular in self-improvement circles; claimed benefits lack supporting evidence per researchers.
note: Researchers say prolonged abstinence may worsen existing mental health problems; the NoFap community has been linked by scholars to manosphere ideas.
currentQuick:
This practice covers avoiding pornography, masturbation and other highly stimulating habits, with the aim of improving focus, confidence, attractiveness or mood. Communities such as NoFap and the 'dopamine fasting' trend frame it as resetting the brain's reward system.
In looksmaxxing circles, abstaining is often listed as a free self-improvement step alongside fitness and skincare. Proponents describe benefits such as willpower and confidence, while researchers report little supporting evidence.
How it works: Proponents say removing high-stimulation activities reduces impulsive behaviour and restores sensitivity to ordinary rewards. The psychologist who developed dopamine fasting, Cameron Sepah, has said the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours rather than literally lower dopamine. Critics note that dopamine is vital and that avoiding a stimulus does not reset it.
Risks and caveats: Surveys found members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than to abstinence, and some researchers argue prolonged abstinence may worsen distress. Extreme versions such as sensory deprivation are criticised by clinicians. DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction.
deepLead:
Dopamine and porn avoidance refers to abstaining from pornography, masturbation and other stimulating behaviours in order to improve self-control, mood or perceived attractiveness. Two overlapping movements are involved: NoFap, an online community founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread, and dopamine fasting, developed by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural tool .
Proponents describe benefits such as better relationships, willpower, self-improvement and so-called superpowers; Wikipedia reports the most prominent claimed benefits lack supporting evidence and that experts describe many NoFap views as simplistic or unsupported . Regarding dopamine fasting, neuroscientists have criticised the idea of a dopamine 'reset', and Sepah says the goal is reducing impulsive behaviours rather than literally lowering dopamine .

name: Alpha / sigma male frameworks

chain: Adopt a dominant or lone-wolf identity
angle.text: Manosphere and looksmaxxing forum users sort men into alpha, beta and sigma types and adopt the high-status archetypes in the hope of seeming more attractive. The typology is borrowed from animal-behaviour research and is not an established model of human social life.

summary: Informal alpha/beta/sigma ranking of men, borrowed from animal behavior; popular online, not an established model of human society.
note: Often tied to manosphere ideology; researchers describe the animal-to-human mapping as an oversimplification.
currentQuick:
Alpha, beta and sigma are labels that online men's communities use to rank men by perceived dominance and status. Sigma refers to a solitary high-status man outside the hierarchy and is now often used ironically.
The terms came from animal-behavior research and were popularised by media and pickup-artist books from the 1990s and 2000s.
How it works: The frameworks are descriptive labels rather than methods. Believers use them to interpret social success, attraction and appearance as products of rank.
Risks and caveats: Researchers describe the human application as an oversimplification, and note that prestige and warmth feature more than dominance in studies of attraction. The labels are sometimes used pejoratively within manosphere communities.
deepLead:
Alpha, beta and sigma male frameworks are informal typologies that sort men into social ranks, usually in online men's communities such as the manosphere, pickup-artist circles and looksmaxxing forums. "Alpha" denotes a dominant, high-status man, "beta" a lower-status or deferential one, and "sigma" a solitary, high-status "lone wolf" who operates outside the hierarchy. The terms are borrowed from animal-behavior research on mating access, territory and feeding order.
Popularisation of "alpha" in human contexts is commonly traced to media usage in the 1990s and to the 2005 pickup-artist book The Game; the "sigma" label first appeared in a blog post and spread widely as a meme after 2021, with much of its later use being ironic. In looksmaxxing discussion the frameworks are often linked to appearance, as in claims that looks, frame and status determine a man's rank.
Scientists quoted in reference works describe applying animal dominance hierarchies to humans as a significant oversimplification, and research on human attraction emphasises prestige and warmth more than dominance.

name: Social proof / status maxxing

chain: Others read you as higher status
angle.text: Users build visible signals such as followers, group photos and high-status associations to raise how attractive they seem. The psychology of social proof is well studied, while the looksmaxxing tactics built on it are untested.

summary: Raising perceived status through social signals; the psychology of social proof is well established, the looksmaxxing tactics are untested.
note: Evidence is for social proof in general, not for these specific tactics.
currentQuick:
Social proof and status maxxing mean using signs of other people's approval and rank, such as friends, followers or associations, to look more attractive or high-status.
Social proof is a well-documented psychological effect; the looksmaxxing applications have not been studied directly.
How it works: People tend to follow others' cues when unsure, and to defer to those with higher perceived status. Practitioners try to display such cues.
Risks and caveats: No medical risks. Effects depend on context and culture, and research notes social proof often produces compliance without private belief.
deepLead:
Social proof, as a looksmaxxing concept, refers to using signals of other people's approval, such as followers, friends, group photos, endorsements and association with high-status people, to raise perceived status and attractiveness. "Status maxxing" is the related idea of improving one's rank in social hierarchies alongside, or instead of, physical appearance.
The underlying psychology is established: social proof is the tendency to copy others' behavior when unsure how to act, a term coined by Robert Cialdini in 1984. Social status itself is the relative social value a person is considered to have, including respect, assumed competence and deference. Whether the specific tactics promoted online change dating or career outcomes has not been tested directly.

name: Money maxxing / career maxxing

chain: Offset or outweigh looks in dating
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and manosphere communities present income and career success as a route to attractiveness, especially for men who see their looks as fixed. Mate-preference research partly supports a link between status and desirability, but the strategy itself has not been tested.

summary: The idea that income and career success can offset or replace looks; supported in part by mate-preference research, untested as a strategy.
note: Evidence concerns status and attractiveness generally, not the strategy itself.
currentQuick:
Money maxxing and career maxxing refer to pursuing income and professional success as a route to status and attractiveness, as an alternative or addition to improving looks.
Reference works report that status and resources influence mate preferences and that looks affect career opportunities, but the strategy has not been tested directly.
How it works: The theory is that wealth and achievement raise perceived status, which influences attraction and also funds appearance improvements.
Risks and caveats: No direct health risks. Outcomes vary by person and culture, and research findings are correlational.
deepLead:
Money maxxing and career maxxing describe the idea in looksmaxxing and manosphere communities that income, wealth and professional success can compensate for, or substitute for, physical attractiveness. It is often presented as an alternative route to status for men who consider their looks fixed.
Research in evolutionary psychology reports that women's mate preferences track indicators of status and resources, and one cited study found that higher-salaried men were rated more attractive. Wikipedia also notes research linking perceived attractiveness to employment outcomes. Whether deliberate career or money strategies change dating outcomes has not been tested as a looksmaxxing practice.

name: Smile practice / smile maxxing

chain: Face looks warmer and more attractive
angle.text: Users rehearse their smile in a mirror to look more genuine and symmetrical, drawing on the difference between polite and genuine smiles. Smile perception has been studied, but smile training itself has not.

summary: Training a more natural, appealing smile; smile perception research exists, but smile training itself is unstudied.
note: Perceived effects of smiling vary by culture.
currentQuick:
Smile maxxing means practicing and refining one's smile, usually in a mirror, to look warmer or more attractive.
Studies show smiles influence how likable people seem, and that genuine and posed smiles differ, but no trials test smile training as such.
How it works: Practitioners aim to use the muscles around the eyes as well as the mouth. Facial feedback research suggests expressions may slightly affect mood.
Risks and caveats: No medical risks reported. Cultural context affects how smiles are read.
deepLead:
Smile practice, or smile maxxing, is the practice of training one's smile, often in a mirror, to look more natural, symmetrical or attractive. Community discussion focuses on the difference between a polite and a genuine smile and on how smiling is perceived.
Research distinguishes the Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eyes, from the voluntary "Pan Am" smile using only the mouth muscle. Studies report smiling can make people seem more likable and approachable, though perceptions differ across cultures. The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that expressions also influence emotion; a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies found small but robust effects.

name: Posture / frame / body language

angle.text: Users hold an upright, open stance, sometimes as power posing, so they look taller and more confident while standing. The visual change is immediately visible; claims about hormone and behaviour shifts from posing have replicated poorly, though effects on how people feel are better supported.

summary: Open, upright body language to look and feel more confident; feelings effects hold up, hormone and behavior claims do not replicate well.
currentQuick:
Posture and body language practices aim to project confidence through upright, open and expansive stances.
Studies show small effects on how powerful people feel, but the hormonal and behavioral effects reported in 2010 have not replicated well.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is postural feedback: body position influencing mood and self-evaluation.
Risks and caveats: No direct risks reported. Ongoing disagreement exists about effect sizes.
deepLead:
In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, "posture", "frame" and "body language" refer to how a person holds and moves the body, with the belief that upright, open and expansive postures make a person look and feel more confident and attractive. "Power posing" is a closely related and widely publicised version.
Research on posture reports that confident postures can influence self-evaluation and mood, but the hormonal and behavioral claims of power posing have not replicated well. Reviews find a reliable effect on feelings of power but not on physiology.

name: Photo comparison / flip test

chain: Spot which side or version looks better
angle.text: Users flip photos or compare them with their mirror image to understand why they look different in pictures and to pick the more flattering version. It relates to the mere exposure effect, though the method itself has not been tested.

summary: Comparing a face with its mirror image to judge looks; related to mere exposure, but the method itself is untested.
note: Perception differences are not clinically validated.
currentQuick:
The flip test means comparing your photo with a horizontally flipped copy, or with the mirror image, to see which looks better and how others may see you.
No published studies have tested the practice itself.
How it works: Believers say familiarity with the mirror image shapes preference; the mere-exposure effect is the related research.
Risks and caveats: No physical risks. Some community members report distress from close self-scrutiny, though this has not been studied here.
deepLead:
The photo comparison or flip test is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person compares photos of themselves with their mirror image, or flips a photo horizontally, to judge which version looks better or to understand why they look different in pictures than in the mirror.
No studies found directly testing the practice. Related psychology includes the mere-exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking, first studied by Zajonc in 1968. Reference works also describe facial symmetry as an attractiveness factor.

name: Mirror flip / symmetry test

chain: Flip a face photo or split halves
angle.text: Users reverse a face photo or compare its two halves to assess symmetry, one of several features in facial analysis. Symmetry features in attractiveness research, but this self-test has not been validated.

summary: Flip your photo and compare the halves; symmetry matters in attractiveness research, but this self-test itself is unvalidated.
note: Mirror composites can create artificial features; no study validates the test.
currentQuick:
The mirror flip test means comparing a face photo with its left-right reversed copy to look at symmetry. It is a common self-check in facial-analysis content.
Research links facial symmetry with attractiveness ratings, but nothing published has tested this specific method.
How it works: People reverse a photo horizontally or build composites from each half of the face and compare them with the original, looking for differences in features.
Risks and caveats: Researchers note that mirrored composites can create artificial features, and natural expression adds temporary asymmetry. Appearance-rating practices have been linked in press coverage to body dysmorphia concerns.[2]
deepLead:
The mirror flip or symmetry test is a self-assessment practice in which a person compares a photograph of their face with its left-right reversed copy, or compares the two halves of the face, to judge how symmetrical it looks. It belongs to the facial-analysis side of looksmaxxing, where symmetry is one of several features people assess.
Published research treats facial symmetry as one of three factors, with averageness and youthfulness, that influence judgments of attractiveness. Studies reported in the 1990s and 2000s found that more symmetrical faces tend to be rated as more attractive, with a larger effect for female faces.
Researchers have also noted that creating symmetric composites by mirroring one half of a face can introduce artificial features, so conclusions drawn from mirrored images have been questioned. No published study has evaluated the mirror flip test as a self-assessment method.

name: Facial analysis YouTube channels

angle.text: Viewers watch creators rate faces on feature scales such as PSL to learn which features to improve and how. The ratings are unvalidated, and press coverage links the content to body-image concerns.

summary: Creators rate faces on feature scales like PSL; popular in the scene, unvalidated, and linked by press to body-image concerns.
note: Press coverage links appearance-rating communities with body dysmorphia.
currentQuick:
Facial analysis channels are creators who break down and rate faces, often using community scales like PSL. They are part of looksmaxxing's online culture.
The ratings are not scientifically validated, and critics call parts of the scale pseudoscientific.
How it works: Creators assess features such as eye tilt, jawline and cheeks, then assign a tier or score and suggest changes, from skincare to surgery.
Risks and caveats: Press coverage has linked appearance-rating communities with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. No studies have examined the content itself.
deepLead:
Facial analysis content is video and livestream material in which creators assess faces, rating features such as eye shape, jawline and cheeks, often against community scales like the PSL scale. It is a staple of looksmaxxing culture online.
Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes the practice as spreading from incel-era forums to TikTok in the 2020s and names livestreamers such as Clavicular and Androgenic; it does not discuss YouTube channels specifically. Critics describe PSL-style ratings as pseudoscientific, and press coverage has linked appearance-rating communities to body dysmorphia.
No studies have examined facial analysis channels or their viewers.

name: Anti-looksmax / 'touch grass' critiques

angle.text: Journalists, researchers and clinicians argue looksmaxxing can be harmful, while the informal 'touch grass' version urges absorbed users to go outside. Within the scene it is read as a counterweight to over-focus on looks, and the benefits it suggests are anecdotal.

summary: The counter-discourse: journalists and researchers criticize looksmaxxing, while 'touch grass' is the informal version.
currentQuick:
This entry covers criticism of looksmaxxing, from academic and press critiques to the casual 'touch grass' jab.
Critics cite anecdote-based claims, injury risks and ties to incel ideology, while practitioners may see the criticism differently.
How it works: Critique appears in journalism, academic papers and online replies telling heavy users to go outside.
Risks and caveats: No direct risks; the topic concerns reported harms such as body dysmorphia and injuries from practices like bonesmashing.
deepLead:
Critiques of looksmaxxing come from journalists, researchers, clinicians and others who argue the practice is harmful or misguided; a common informal version tells practitioners to 'touch grass', a phrase meaning go outside, used mockingly at people who seem absorbed in online content.
Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article records several lines of criticism: that the movement is judgmental, that mewing and 'bonesmashing' are regarded as misinformation by doctors and researchers, that it relies on anecdote and promotes male supremacy, and that it may channel young men toward incel views.

name: Therapy for looks-related anxiety (ACT)

angle.text: Acceptance and commitment therapy is raised in looksmaxxing discussions as a way to handle appearance anxiety so it interferes less with daily life and social presence. ACT is well studied generally, though it has not been tested within looksmaxxing.

summary: A mindfulness-based therapy sometimes suggested for appearance anxiety; well studied generally, untested for looksmaxxing.
note: General ACT evidence is mixed versus CBT for anxiety.
currentQuick:
ACT is a talk therapy that teaches accepting unwanted thoughts and acting on personal values. It is discussed as an option for anxiety about appearance.
It has a large general research base, but no study here tests it for looksmaxxing-related anxiety.
How it works: Through mindfulness and values exercises, people learn to notice thoughts without acting on them and to pursue valued activities despite discomfort.
Risks and caveats: ACT is generally a low-risk talk therapy. Critics question whether its distinctive components drive its effects.
deepLead:
Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) is a form of cognitive behavioral therapy that uses mindfulness to help people notice thoughts and feelings, accept them rather than fight them, and commit to actions based on personal values. In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a psychological approach to appearance-related anxiety.
ACT was developed by Steven C. Hayes in the 1980s and formally described in a 1999 book. The wider ACT literature has grown to more than 1,000 randomized trials, with mixed findings against standard CBT for anxiety and depression. No study located here tests ACT specifically for looks-related anxiety in looksmaxxing contexts.

name: Antidepressants / anxiety meds

angle.text: Prescription antidepressants and anxiety medicines are discussed in the scene as aids for social anxiety and low mood that can hold back confidence. They are prescribed for mental-health conditions rather than appearance, and an appearance benefit is anecdotal.

summary: Rx mental-health drugs used for anxiety and depression; not appearance treatments, with modest effects and real side effects.
note: FDA warning on suicidality in young people; discontinuation symptoms reported.
currentQuick:
Antidepressants are prescription drugs for depression and anxiety disorders. In looksmaxxing they appear as a medication option for appearance-related distress.
They are not appearance treatments, and no study tests them for that.
How it works: Most block reuptake of serotonin, sometimes with norepinephrine, raising signaling in the brain.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include sexual dysfunction, weight change and emotional blunting. An FDA warning covers suicidal thinking in under-25s, and stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms. Prescription only.
deepLead:
Antidepressants are prescription drugs used mainly for major depressive disorder and also for anxiety disorders such as generalized and social anxiety, panic disorder, OCD and PTSD. Main classes include SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs.
Meta-analyses find they outperform placebo in depression by a modest margin; for anxiety disorders the drug-placebo effect size is about 0.3. They are not appearance treatments and no study tests them for looksmaxxing-related concerns. Common adverse effects include sexual dysfunction, weight change and emotional blunting.

name: Psychedelic therapy for self-image

angle.text: Some forum users float psilocybin, LSD or MDMA therapy as a way to reshape how they see their own appearance. Research has focused on depression, PTSD and anxiety, and no direct body-image studies exist.

summary: Experimental idea of using psychedelics for body image; no direct studies, and the drugs are controlled substances.
note: Schedule I in the US; contraindicated with some medications and psychiatric histories.
currentQuick:
Psychedelic therapy uses drugs like psilocybin with guided sessions to treat mental health conditions. Using it for self-image is experimental.
No studies directly examine self-image outcomes.
How it works: Mechanisms are poorly understood; outcomes depend heavily on mindset and setting.
Risks and caveats: The drugs are Schedule I in the US. Contraindications include psychosis history, pregnancy and SSRI use.
deepLead:
Psychedelic therapy is the proposed use of drugs such as psilocybin, LSD and MDMA in mental health treatment, usually with preparation and integration sessions. Its use for self-image is an experimental idea; research has focused on depression, PTSD, anxiety and substance use.
The only item related to body image on the source page is a 2024 review in which a single psilocybin dose given for OCD symptoms raised insight in patients who also had body dysmorphic disorder, leading them to seek treatment. Psychedelics remain Schedule I in the US and are generally limited to clinical trials.

name: Social media dysmorphia (filter dysmorphia / Snapchat dysmorphia)

angle.text: The term describes people who want to look like their filtered selfies, which drives interest in cosmetic procedures and in how photos are framed. Studies link filter use to body dissatisfaction and surgery interest, though it is an informal term and not a formal diagnosis.

summary: Informal name for wanting to look like your filtered selfie; linked in studies to body dissatisfaction and surgery interest, but not a formal diagnosis.
note: Evidence is mostly correlational; not a formal diagnosis.
currentQuick:
Social media dysmorphia describes people feeling distress about, or seeking cosmetic procedures to match, their filtered selfies. The term was coined by surgeon Tijion Esho.
It is an informal label, not a diagnosis, and is discussed alongside body dysmorphic disorder.
How it works: Filters smooth skin and reshape features in real time, which commentators say creates an idealised self-image that real appearance cannot match. Observational studies link photo editing and image-focused platform use to body dissatisfaction.
Risks and caveats: Researchers link heavy editing and platform use to body preoccupation and surgery consideration, though causation is unproven. Surgeons are urged to screen for BDD, and cosmetic surgery is not considered a treatment for it.
deepLead:
Social media dysmorphia, also called Snapchat dysmorphia, filter dysmorphia or selfie dysmorphia, is an informal term for the phenomenon of people seeking cosmetic procedures to resemble their filtered or edited selfies, or feeling distress at the gap between their real appearance and edited images of themselves. It is not a formal diagnosis. Clinicians discuss it in relation to body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), an obsessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance.
The term was coined by British cosmetic surgeon Tijion Esho, who observed that patients had shifted from bringing photos of celebrities to bringing edited images of themselves. Research links heavy use of image-based platforms and photo-editing to body dissatisfaction and greater willingness to consider cosmetic surgery, though much of the evidence is correlational.

name: Beauty privilege research (pretty premium)

angle.text: Looksmaxxers cite labour-economics findings that more attractive people tend to get better hiring and pay outcomes as a reason to invest in appearance. The premium is documented in research, while its size and causes are still debated.

summary: Economic research finding that better-looking people earn and get hired somewhat more; effect sizes and causes are debated.
note: Studies are observational or résumé experiments and do not show that specific looks changes raise earnings.
currentQuick:
The pretty premium is the research finding that people rated more attractive tend to be hired more and paid more. The landmark study, by Hamermesh and Biddle, reported a plainness penalty of about 5 to 10 percent in earnings.
Later résumé experiments in Argentina, Israel and Peru found callback advantages for attractive applicants, with patterns that differ by country and sex.
How it works: Researchers propose several explanations, including halo-effect bias, employer or customer preferences, and productivity in jobs involving interpersonal contact. Which explanation applies is debated.
Risks and caveats: The research is a body of findings rather than a practice, so it carries no direct physical risk. Critics argue that appearance preferences are evolved or productivity-related and not clearly an injustice, while some jurisdictions, such as Belgium, have laws covering appearance-based discrimination.
deepLead:
The 'pretty premium' or beauty premium refers to the finding, reported in labour-economics and psychology research, that people rated as more physically attractive tend to receive better outcomes in hiring and pay than people rated as less attractive. The idea is often called 'pretty privilege' or 'lookism' in popular and online usage. 
The best-known early study is the 1993 to 1994 paper 'Beauty and the Labor Market' by Daniel Hamermesh and Jeff Biddle, which used US and Canadian surveys in which interviewers rated respondents' appearance. They reported that plain-looking people earned less than average-looking people, who earned less than good-looking people, with a plainness penalty of about 5 to 10 percent, somewhat larger than the beauty premium, and with effects somewhat larger for men than for women. 
Later field experiments sent fictitious résumés with photographs and compared callbacks, with mixed patterns by country and sex. Researchers also dispute how the results should be interpreted, and some authors argue that appearance preferences may reflect evolved tendencies or productivity rather than injustice.  In looksmaxxing culture, the research is cited as a rationale for improving appearance. Community discussion of it was not available for this entry.

name: Evolutionary psychology of attractiveness

chain: Targets for face and body changes
angle.text: Looksmaxxers draw on evolutionary accounts of beauty to decide which features, such as symmetry and sexual dimorphism, to prioritise. Support in research is mixed and contested.

summary: The theory that beauty preferences are evolved mate-choice adaptations; often cited online, with mixed and contested support in research.
note: Correlations between features and health are debated, and samples are often narrow.
currentQuick:
Evolutionary psychologists propose that preferences for symmetry, averageness, sexual dimorphism and certain body ratios evolved because they signalled health or genetic quality.
The framework is often cited in looksmaxxing discussions to explain why some features are rated highly.
How it works: The idea is that natural and sexual selection shaped specialised mate-choice mechanisms in the brain, which respond to cues linked to fertility and health.
Risks and caveats: No clinical risks apply. Critics note weak or inconsistent links between attractive features and health, cultural variation in preferences, and studies limited to narrow samples.
deepLead:
The evolutionary psychology of attractiveness is the study of human beauty preferences as products of natural and sexual selection. Evolutionary psychology treats the mind as made of specialised mechanisms shaped to solve recurring ancestral problems, including choosing mates. Within this framework, researchers have proposed that preferences for features such as facial symmetry, averageness, sexual dimorphism and particular body ratios evolved because they signalled health, fertility or genetic quality.
The approach is widely cited in looksmaxxing and related online communities to justify why certain features are rated highly. Critics within science question whether the correlations between attractive features and health are strong, and point to cultural variation and sampling limits.

name: Spreader grafts

angle.text: Surgeons place these cartilage strips during rhinoplasty to keep the middle of the nose straight and the bridge lines smooth after a hump is reduced. The reshaping is visible once healed; evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series.

summary: Cartilage strips placed beside the septum to open the internal nasal valve and keep the nose bridge straight after hump reduction; supported mainly by surgeon case series.
note: Part of rhinoplasty; revision surgery is reported in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties.
currentQuick:
Spreader grafts are small strips of cartilage, usually from the septum, placed along the nasal bridge during rhinoplasty. Surgeons use them to widen the internal nasal valve, keep the bridge straight and avoid a pinched mid-nose after a hump is reduced.
The evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers, with a few registered trials.
How it works: The graft holds the upper lateral cartilages away from the septum, widening the angle of the internal nasal valve and preserving smooth dorsal lines.
Risks and caveats: It is done under general rhinoplasty risks, and revision rhinoplasty accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases. Graft-specific complication rates were not reported in the sources reviewed. It is a surgical procedure performed only by clinicians.
deepLead:
Spreader grafts are thin strips of cartilage, usually taken from the nasal septum, that surgeons place between the septum and the upper lateral cartilages during rhinoplasty. They are used to widen the internal nasal valve, support or straighten the middle third of the nose, and keep the dorsal aesthetic lines smooth after a dorsal hump has been reduced .
Reduction of a dorsal hump often disrupts the junction of the septum and upper lateral cartilages (sometimes called the keystone area), and surgeons describe spreader grafts or spreader flaps as ways to rebuild it for both appearance and breathing . Surgeons also publish techniques intended to lessen the need for them, such as component dorsal reduction that preserves the upper lateral cartilages .
Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and technique descriptions. At least one registered randomized trial has compared outcomes with and without spreader grafts in reduction rhinoseptoplasty with a quality-of-life measure, but its results are not published in the sources reviewed here .

name: Columellar strut graft

angle.text: Rhinoplasty patients get this concealed cartilage support to hold the nasal tip in a defined position. The change is visible after healing, though surgeons debate how much it raises the tip compared with septal extension grafts.

summary: A hidden cartilage post under the nasal tip that supports it; surgeons debate how much it raises the tip and compare it with septal extension grafts.
note: Part of rhinoplasty; roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties are revisions.
currentQuick:
A columellar strut is a small cartilage graft placed between the lower nose cartilages to give the nasal tip support during rhinoplasty. It is invisible after healing.
Surgeons have long assumed it increases tip projection, though a 100-case review examined that assumption directly, and many surgeons now also use septal extension grafts.
How it works: The strut acts as a post between the medial crura, helping hold the tip in position and maintain its shape.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general, and revision surgery accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations. Graft-specific rates were not reported in the sources reviewed. It is a surgical procedure.
deepLead:
A columellar strut graft is a piece of cartilage placed between the medial crura of the lower lateral cartilages in the columella, the strip of tissue between the nostrils, during rhinoplasty to support the nasal tip. Surgeons describe it as a popular form of invisible graft because it is hidden beneath the skin .
It has traditionally been assumed to increase tip projection, but a retrospective review of 100 consecutive primary rhinoplasties examined its actual effect on tip projection and rotation . Surgeons have also compared the strut with the caudal septal extension graft, which some describe as offering more control of tip position .
The evidence is mainly surgeon case series and comparative retrospective studies, along with some small registered trials.
